greeting: Good morning, Bay View. It's a gift of a November Thursday: sunny and mild, with a high near 63 and a southwest breeze. Today we've got a new plan for the I-794 spur that keeps the Hoan's link to downtown, a master hatter on KK and the woman who started Bay View's first library.

top.title: Rethink 794's new boulevard plan keeps the Hoan Bridge connection to downtown
top.dek: The advocates' 'Better Boulevard' would replace the I-794 spur and free 8 more acres than the state's plan.
top.body:
Rethink 794, the volunteer group pushing to replace the elevated I-794 spur between downtown and the Third Ward with a street-level boulevard, released a redesigned "Better Boulevard Plan" on Wednesday and sent it to WisDOT and city officials.

The group says its version uses existing ramps instead of rebuilding redundant connections near the Marquette Interchange. That, it says, would cut costs and open about 24 acres for development, compared with 16 under the state's boulevard option. For South Shore commuters, the group says the Hoan Bridge would still give the same access to downtown it does now. One volunteer put it simply: "Exit the Hoan Bridge from the south, and you're Downtown."

WisDOT is still weighing three options: rebuild as-is ($425-575 million), a slimmer elevated freeway ($675 million-$1 billion), or a boulevard ($850 million-$1.25 billion). Mayor Cavalier Johnson backed the slimmer freeway in July. The group will hold a free public forum on Dec. 1 at UWM.

image.alt: Rethink 794's map of its proposed boulevard through downtown, with an arrow marking access from the Hoan Bridge

top.title: City must spend its last federal pandemic dollars by year's end, and Bay View's alder wants a say
top.dek: About $1.1 million in ARPA money is at risk of going back to Washington; council and mayor disagree on where it goes.
top.body:
Milwaukee has until Dec. 31 to spend the rest of its $394 million American Rescue Plan Act grant or return the money to Washington. City staff told the Finance & Personnel Committee on Wednesday that about $1.1 million, and possibly as much as $1.8 million, is at risk.

Most of that money had been set aside for COVID-19 vaccines and tests that the Health Department says it can no longer use or store. Another roughly $140,000 was meant for demolitions.

Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic, who represents Bay View and chairs the committee, wants the leftover money sent to the City Clerk's Office, which would put it under council control. The budget office would rather move it to Public Works so the city borrows less, possibly by covering salaries already paid. The full Common Council next meets Tuesday, Nov. 24.

image.alt: Milwaukee City Hall's clock tower seen from above, with downtown streets behind it

development.title: Bay View's busiest development group buys four century-old duplexes at Delaware and Iron
development.dek: The cluster at Delaware Avenue and Iron Street dates to 1905; no plans for it have been filed.
development.body:
An investor group that Urban Milwaukee calls Bay View's most active development group has bought four more homes, a cluster of early-1900s duplexes at the corner of S. Delaware Avenue and E. Iron Street, the site reported Wednesday.

City property records show a single LLC owned four duplexes at that corner: 2643, 2647 and 2651 S. Delaware Ave. and 1614 E. Iron St. All were built in 1905 or 1906, and together they are assessed at about $1.65 million. Most of Urban Milwaukee's report, including the buyer's plans, is for members only.

No permits or zoning requests for the site have been filed. Any demolition or new building would need city approval, so watch for public notices. The Bulletin will report on any plans once they're public.

image.alt: A two-story frame duplex with a front porch on a tree-lined Bay View corner

development.hold_reason: Urban Milwaukee's report is members-only (paywalled), so the buyer and plans are unknown; matching the sale to the four Delaware/Iron duplexes is our inference from city property records, not confirmed. Run only if you can confirm from a free source.

parks.title: County golf courses, including nearby Grant Park, stay open through at least Sunday
parks.dek: Eight Milwaukee County courses are still taking tee times thanks to the warm fall, and could stay open longer.
parks.body:
The mild weather is giving golfers extra rounds. Milwaukee County Parks is keeping eight courses open through at least Sunday, Nov. 22, Urban Milwaukee reported Wednesday.

The full-size courses at Brown Deer, Dretzka, Lincoln, Oakwood and Grant parks are taking tee-time reservations. Grant Park, in South Milwaukee, is the closest to Bay View. The par-3 courses at Noyes, Lake and Zablocki parks are open too. Parks says the season could run longer if conditions hold.

The extra weeks help the whole park system: golf brought in about 23% of the Parks budget in 2025. County courses have logged more than 390,000 rounds and more than $12 million in revenue so far in 2026, both records.

image.alt: A flag on a green at Lake Park Golf Course, with fallen leaves and autumn trees

sports.title: The Blue Angels will be back over the lakefront for next July's Air & Water Show
sports.dek: The Navy jets skipped the 2026 show; they flew in Wednesday to confirm their 2027 return.
sports.body:
The U.S. Navy Blue Angels will headline the Milwaukee Air & Water Show next July, the team announced Wednesday at the 128th Air Refueling Wing near Mitchell Airport.

The team skipped this year's show. Next summer, six F/A-18 Super Hornets will fly over Lake Michigan along the downtown lakefront. A team pilot promised a show much like the ones past crowds have seen.

Exact dates and other details will come later from show organizers.

spotlight.title: Spotlight: McLaughlin & Hayes Hat Co.
spotlight.dek: Bay View's master hatters still block felt on century-old equipment, and won't sell you a hat online
spotlight.body:
Inside the former Boulevard Theatre at 2250 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. is something most cities lost decades ago: a working hat shop. McLaughlin & Hayes Hat Co. sells, makes, cleans and repairs hats for men and women, from fedoras and western hats to Derby showpieces and fascinators.

John and Kate McLaughlin opened the business in 2011 as the Brass Rooster, a men's hat shop on the Avalon Theater block. In late 2014 they moved down the street into the larger former Boulevard Theatre space and added the Hen House, a women's shop, next door. The two later merged under the McLaughlin & Hayes name, with Steve Hayes joining the McLaughlins as a co-owner. Kate spent 10 seasons as the Milwaukee Rep's hatmaker and costume craft manager; John has worn and reshaped hats since he found his grandfather's fedora as a kid.

The shop says it is home to three of roughly 15 master hatters left in the country. Custom hats are built in house after a measuring and design consultation, usually in four to six weeks, on century-old equipment that came from a retiring hatter at Henry the Hatter in Detroit. The racks also carry makers like Stetson, Bailey, Dobbs and Kangol. Repair work is done on site too: cleaning and blocking felt hats, new ribbons, brim trims, leather sweatbands and full rebuilds. One thing you can't do is order online. The owners stopped web sales so every customer talks to a person, though they still take orders by phone and ship worldwide. "A hat is like a haircut you get to put on every day," John told TMJ4.

The work travels. The shop has made headwear for stage and screen, including the Tony-winning Broadway musical "War Paint," the Metropolitan Opera and Netflix's "Peaky Blinders," and one of its fedoras had a starring role in a 2020 Super Bowl ad about Vince Lombardi. John also developed a hand-inked technique that turns felt hats into painted art. For the Kentucky Derby's 150th running in 2024, one of those, a beaver-felt fedora painted with a horse race scene, was picked from worldwide entries for the Kentucky Derby Museum's permanent collection.

With cold weather settling in, this is the season for wool and fur felt, and for getting an old favorite cleaned and reblocked. Appointments are no longer required but are still recommended for custom fittings, since they book a week or two out.

McLaughlin & Hayes Hat Co., 2250 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. Open Tuesday-Saturday 11 a.m.-5 p.m. 414-210-3715, mhhats.com, @mhhatmilmke on Instagram.

history.title: Beulah Brinton, the mill town's teacher, librarian and neighbor
history.text: In 1872, Beulah Brinton moved into a new house on Superior Street and opened it to the rolling mill's immigrant families. Her lending library grew into Milwaukee's first branch library.
history.body:
In 1872, Beulah Brinton arrived in Bay View from Michigan with her husband, Warren, who took a job at the Milwaukee Iron Company's rolling mill. The mill was founded by her cousin, Eber Brock Ward. The couple settled into a frame house at what is now 2590 S. Superior St., built for them in 1870 and 1871.

Bay View was then a company town full of newly arrived iron workers and their families. Brinton turned her home into a gathering place. She taught English and reading to mill workers' wives and children, along with sewing, cooking and music, and sometimes worked as a midwife. She raised money for books, which mill owner Ward matched, and lent them from her house. That collection of some 300 volumes is counted as Bay View's first public library. It later moved to the first branch of the Milwaukee Public Library and became the core of today's Bay View library.

She was a writer, too. She published a Civil War novel, "Man Is Love," in the 1870s, edited a local paper, the Bay View Herald, and preached at her Methodist church. She is credited with bringing tennis to the neighborhood, with a court on the empty lot beside her house. After the 1886 shootings at the mill during the eight-hour strike, she led prayer gatherings to help the neighborhood heal.

Warren Brinton died in 1895, and Beulah later moved to Chicago to live with her son. While she was away, the historical society says, she rented the house to a family whose son grew up to be the actor Spencer Tracy. In 1924 the city named Bay View's first social center, in an old firehouse on St. Clair Street, after her. She came home to Bay View after a stroke in 1926 and died in March 1928 at about 92. Sources differ on whether she was born in 1835 or 1836.

The Beulah Brinton Community Center on Bay Street, opened in 1981, still carries her name. Her house is now the headquarters of the Bay View Historical Society, and the lot beside it, where she once played tennis, is still empty.
history.source_name: Encyclopedia of Milwaukee, "Beulah Brinton" (William I. Tchakirides)
